subject: A few things I noticed about Rick's Automotive's online presence
body:
Hi there,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Rick's Automotive Center and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- You've got more forms in place than most shops — appointment request, drop-off, even an 'Ask the Mechanic' form. And 35 years in business is a story worth telling louder.
- A testimonial on the contact page shows you're proud of the work.

Where you're leaving money on the table
- No after-hours capture. You're closed Fri-Sun and evenings, so anyone who finds you then hits a form and waits — no instant callback catching the lead while they're deciding. Closing three days a week makes that gap bigger than it is for most shops.
- Your email isn't even clickable on the page, and it's a free verizon.net address — beyond looking dated, those can land in spam when you email customers. A branded address on your own domain would fix both.
- No live chat. A lot of customers won't call — they'll ask a quick question in a chat box or leave.
- The site is missing the behind-the-scenes setup (LocalBusiness markup) that tells Google to surface you for "auto repair near me" searches — so you're likely ranking below newer shops.

None of this is urgent, and the shop clearly has staying power — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

Best,
Leo Lebel
cheddar.lebel@gmail.com

subject: A few things I noticed about Chris Amato's Body Werks' online presence
body:
Hi Chris,

I run a small studio that helps local auto body shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across Body Werks and spent some time looking at how you show up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- Sharp niche — luxury and EV (BMW, Mercedes, Tesla, Rivian, Lucid, Porsche) is exactly the high-value work to specialize in, and you've got a free-estimate form and clean behind-the-scenes Google markup already in place. Better setup than most body shops.
- Strong reputation (~184 Yelp reviews at 4.5).

Where you're leaving money on the table
- That 184-review reputation isn't surfaced as a star block on your own site. Someone landing there to decide between you and another shop doesn't see the proof you've earned — pulling it onto the page is a cheap, high-leverage win.
- No online booking. There's an estimate form, but a Tesla owner ready to lock in a drop-off slot can't actually schedule — they wait for a callback.
- No live chat. A lot of estimate-shoppers want a quick answer before they commit to a form.
- No after-hours capture beyond the static form — a collision inquiry at 8pm sits until morning instead of getting an instant callback.

None of this is urgent, and your work clearly speaks for itself — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.

Best,

subject: A few things I noticed about All German Auto's online presence
body:
Hi there,

I run a small studio that helps local auto shops capture more of the work that's already trying to reach them online. I came across All German Auto and spent some time looking at how your Oceanside location shows up on the web. Here's a quick, honest audit — no pitch, just what I found:

What's working
- You're ahead of most shops — online appointment scheduling, a contact form, and customer testimonials right on the site. Manufacturer-certified techs is a strong trust signal too.
- Good reputation (Yelp ~94 reviews on the Oceanside listing).

Where you're leaving money on the table
- The site is missing the behind-the-scenes setup (LocalBusiness markup with hours, location, service type) that tells Google to surface you for "German auto repair near me" searches — so you're likely ranking below shops doing worse work. For a multi-location shop, that's real lost visibility.
- No live chat. A lot of customers want a quick "can you work on my Audi?" answer before they commit to booking.
- No after-hours capture. You're closed evenings and weekends, so a high-ticket inquiry then has no instant callback catching it while they're deciding.

None of this is urgent, and your setup is clearly more dialed-in than most — but each of these is quietly costing you jobs that are already trying to reach you.

If you ever want, I'm happy to walk through how a couple of these could be fixed cheaply. Either way, figured the audit might be useful.
